Volume 6A
AWS Cloud Engineering Foundations
Chapters 1-10
Beginner to Production-Ready DevOps Engineer
Concepts • Architecture • Security • CLI • Labs • Troubleshooting • Interviews
2026 Edition

About This Book
Volume 6A is the foundation component of the AWS Cloud Engineering volume in the DevOps Master
Course series. It is designed to move a learner from cloud fundamentals to the point where they can
deploy, secure, scale, network, and financially govern a small production-style AWS workload. Learning principle: Every chapter explains why the service or design exists before showing how to use
it. The labs deliberately emphasize repeatability, least privilege, validation, and cleanup. Scope and Safety

Use a dedicated learning account wherever possible.

Enable billing alerts before launching resources.

Do not use the root user for daily administration.

Never publish access keys, private keys, passwords, or account identifiers.

Prices, quotas, Free Tier offers, and available features can change. Verify current details in the official
AWS documentation and pricing pages before production use. How to Use the Labs
1. Read the architecture and security sections before opening the console.
2. Perform the task manually once to understand the resource model.
3. Repeat it with the AWS CLI where a CLI exercise is provided.
4. Validate identity, Region, resource tags, security rules, health, logs, and cost exposure.
5. Delete chargeable resources at the end of the lab unless the next lab depends on them.

CHAPTER 1
Cloud Computing and Amazon Web
Services
Why cloud operating models changed modern infrastructure engineering
Learning Objectives

Define cloud computing using operational characteristics rather than marketing language.

Compare on-premises infrastructure with cloud infrastructure.

Distinguish IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, public, private, and hybrid cloud models.

Explain shared responsibility, elasticity, resilience, and consumption-based cost.

Connect AWS services to the DevOps lifecycle.
1.1 Why Cloud Computing Exists
Traditional infrastructure required organizations to predict future demand, purchase servers months in
advance, prepare data-center space, install operating systems, and maintain excess capacity for peak
periods. Forecast errors produced one of two outcomes: insufficient capacity during demand spikes or
expensive idle equipment during normal operation. Cloud computing changes the operating model. Compute, storage, networking, databases, security
controls, and managed platforms can be requested through APIs. Infrastructure therefore becomes
programmable. The important shift is not simply that servers are hosted elsewhere; it is that
infrastructure can be provisioned, measured, automated, replaced, and scaled through software. DevOps connection: Cloud APIs make infrastructure automation possible. CI/CD pipelines,
Infrastructure as Code, policy automation, ephemeral test environments, and automated recovery all
depend on programmable infrastructure.

1.4 Deployment Models

Public cloud: provider-operated infrastructure offered to many customers with logical isolation.

Private cloud: cloud-like automation and self-service dedicated to one organization.

Hybrid cloud: coordinated use of on-premises and public-cloud environments.

Multi-cloud: deliberate use of services from more than one public-cloud provider.
1.5 AWS as a Cloud Platform
AWS exposes infrastructure and managed services through the Management Console, CLI, SDKs, and APIs. The platform spans compute, storage, networking, databases, containers, serverless computing, security,
observability, analytics, and developer tooling. A DevOps engineer must understand both individual
services and the operational relationships between them.
1.6 Shared Responsibility Model
AWS secures the infrastructure that runs AWS services. Customers secure their workloads, identities, data,
configurations, guest operating systems where applicable, and application behavior. The exact boundary
changes by service type: the customer manages more for EC2 than for a highly managed serverless
service.

ities, data,
configurations, guest operating systems where applicable, and application behavior. The exact boundary
changes by service type: the customer manages more for EC2 than for a highly managed serverless
service. Common failure: A managed service does not remove customer responsibility. Public S3 access,
excessive IAM permissions, weak application authentication, and unpatched EC2 operating systems
remain customer-controlled risks.

1.7 Cloud Economics
Cloud replaces large up-front capital expenditure with consumption-oriented operational expenditure, but
it does not guarantee lower cost. Elasticity lowers cost only when resources are right-sized, stopped, scaled
in, deleted, or purchased under suitable pricing models. Unowned resources and permanent
overprovisioning simply move waste into a monthly bill.
1.8 Production Design Principles

Design for failure and automate recovery.

Prefer repeatable deployment over manual configuration.

Deploy across failure boundaries when availability matters.

Use least privilege and short-lived credentials.

Collect metrics, logs, traces, and audit records.

Tag resources and assign cost ownership.

Treat backups as recoverability systems and test restoration. Chapter Summary

Cloud computing is an API-driven operating model, not merely remote hosting.

Elasticity, automation, and measured usage create both engineering opportunities and governance
obligations.

AWS supports the complete DevOps lifecycle, but customers remain responsible for secure workload
configuration. Interview Questions
1. How is cloud computing different from traditional hosting?
2. Explain elasticity versus scalability.
3. Compare IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS using operational responsibility.
4. What does shared responsibility mean for an EC2 workload?
5. Why can a cloud migration increase rather than reduce cost?
6. How does cloud infrastructure enable DevOps practices?

CHAPTER 2
AWS Global Infrastructure
Regions, Availability Zones, edge infrastructure, resilience, and data placement
Learning Objectives

Explain Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations.

Choose a Region using latency, compliance, service availability, resilience, and cost.

Differentiate high availability from disaster recovery.

Design a basic multi-AZ application.

Identify the operational consequences of Region-scoped and global services.
2.1 Regions
An AWS Region is a separate geographic area containing multiple isolated Availability Zones. Many
resources—including VPCs, EC2 instances, EBS volumes, and load balancers—are created in a selected
Region. Region choice is therefore an architectural decision rather than a cosmetic console setting.
2.2 Availability Zones
An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more discrete data centers with independent power, networking, and
physical facilities inside a Region. AZs are connected by high-bandwidth, low-latency links. Deploying
application capacity across multiple AZs reduces dependence on a single facility-level failure domain. Important: Multiple EC2 instances in one Availability Zone improve host redundancy but do not
provide multi-AZ resilience. Failure-domain diversity requires placement across AZs.
2.3 Edge Infrastructure
Edge locations and related AWS edge infrastructure bring services such as content delivery, DNS
resolution, security enforcement, and request acceleration closer to users.

es placement across AZs.
2.3 Edge Infrastructure
Edge locations and related AWS edge infrastructure bring services such as content delivery, DNS
resolution, security enforcement, and request acceleration closer to users. Edge infrastructure is not
interchangeable with an Availability Zone: it serves different networking and delivery purposes.

using multiple AZs. Disaster recovery restores or continues business service after a larger event,
potentially using another Region. Recovery Time Objective (RTO) describes the maximum acceptable time
to restore service. Recovery Point Objective (RPO) describes the maximum acceptable data loss measured

2.8 Operational Checklist

Confirm the active Region before every deployment and destructive action.

Use at least two AZs for production services requiring high availability.

Avoid creating state that can be recovered only from one AZ.

Document RTO and RPO before selecting a disaster-recovery pattern.

Test failover and recovery; architecture diagrams alone do not prove recoverability. Chapter Summary

Regions are geographic boundaries; Availability Zones are isolated failure domains within Regions.

Multi-AZ design supports high availability, while multi-Region design may support disaster recovery
or global service delivery.

Region selection must include compliance, latency, service availability, cost, and resilience. Interview Questions
1. What is the difference between a Region and an Availability Zone?
2. Why is deploying two instances in one AZ not sufficient for multi-AZ availability?
3. Explain RTO and RPO.
4. Compare backup-and-restore with warm standby.
5. What factors would you use to choose an AWS Region?
6. What is the role of edge infrastructure?

3. List the Availability Zones visible to your account in the chosen Region.

CHAPTER 3
AWS Account Setup, Free Usage Controls,
and Root Security
Build a safe learning account before creating infrastructure
Learning Objectives

Secure the root user and configure MFA.

Create an administrative access path without routine root use.

Understand that Free Tier and trial offers have service-specific limits.

Configure cost visibility and alerts.

Apply account-level security and ownership controls.
3.1 Account as a Security Boundary
An AWS account is a billing, ownership, quota, and security boundary. Every resource belongs to an
account. Account setup therefore establishes the foundation for identity, logging, cost controls, support,
and incident response.
3.2 Root User
The root user is created from the account email address and has account-level capabilities that cannot be
fully restricted by ordinary IAM policy. It should be used only for tasks that specifically require root
credentials. Routine console work, CLI access, application access, and automation must use delegated
identities. Root security baseline: Use a unique email address, a unique high-entropy password, phishing-
resistant MFA where practical, secure recovery methods, and monitored use. Do not create root access
keys.
3.3 Initial Security Sequence
1. Enable MFA for the root user.
2. Confirm alternate security, operations, and billing contacts.
3. Create or enable a delegated administrative identity, preferably through AWS IAM Identity Center for
human access.
4. Enable audit logging and centralized log retention as the environment grows.
5. Configure budgets, cost alerts, and anomaly visibility.
6. Sign out of root and test delegated administration.
7. Document the emergency root-access procedure.

3.4 Free Usage Is Not Unlimited
AWS Free Tier, credits, and service trials are not blanket protection from charges. Each offer has eligibility
rules, time periods, Regions, quantities, and service-specific conditions. Data transfer, public IPv4
addresses, storage, snapshots, NAT gateways, load balancers, and idle resources can create charges even in
a learning environment. Cost rule: Treat every resource as chargeable unless the current AWS pricing page explicitly confirms
otherwise for your account and usage.
3.5 Billing and Cost Controls

Enable access to billing information only for approved identities.

Create a small monthly budget with notification thresholds.

Use cost allocation tags such as Project, Environment, Owner, and CostCenter.

Review the billing dashboard after each lab that creates persistent resources.

Delete unused EBS volumes, snapshots, Elastic IP addresses, load balancers, NAT gateways, databases,
and log retention that is no longer needed.
3.6 Account Contacts and Recovery
Security and billing incidents often occur when the primary account owner is unavailable. Organizations
should use role-based contact addresses rather than one employee’s mailbox, protect the email account
with MFA, maintain recovery procedures, and ensure payment and contact details remain current.
3.7 Multi-Account Direction
A single account is acceptable for initial learning, but enterprises normally separate production, non-
production, security, logging, and shared services into multiple accounts governed through AWS
Organizations. Account separation limits blast radius and improves ownership, billing, and policy control.

e production, non-
production, security, logging, and shared services into multiple accounts governed through AWS
Organizations. Account separation limits blast radius and improves ownership, billing, and policy control. Chapter Summary

The root user is an emergency account identity, not a daily administrator.

Free usage controls require active budgets, alerts, and cleanup.

Account contacts, delegated administration, logging, and recovery procedures should be established
before production workloads. Interview Questions
1. Why should the root user not be used for daily work?
2. What account-level actions should be taken immediately after registration?
3. Why can a Free Tier account still receive charges?
4. Why are multi-account environments common in enterprises?
5. What information should an emergency root-access procedure contain?

Hands-on Lab 3 - Secure the Learning Account
Objective: Apply a minimum account security and cost-control baseline. Tasks
1. Enable MFA for the root user and verify that no root access key exists.
2. Configure delegated administrator access and sign in without root.
3. Run the identity check appropriate to the access method.
4. Create a monthly cost budget and at least two notification thresholds.
5. Add alternate security, operations, and billing contacts.
6. Create a written cleanup checklist for all future labs. Validation

Daily administration works without root.

A budget and notification recipients are configured.

Root credentials are stored securely and not used by CLI or applications.


Install and configure AWS CLI v2 safely.

Use named profiles and verify caller identity.

Understand credential provider chains and temporary credentials.

Automate repeatable resource queries and changes.

4.2 Console Discipline

Confirm account alias or account ID and Region before making changes.

Use tags and resource names that make ownership and environment obvious.

Avoid console-only production configuration; capture repeatable state as code.

Use separate browser profiles or clear visual markers for production and non-production accounts.
4.3 AWS CLI Installation and Verification
aws --version
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws configure list
aws configure list-profiles
The identity check returns the account and principal used for the request. Run it before administrative or
destructive commands, especially when multiple profiles or roles are available.

4.4 Named Profiles
aws configure --profile learning-admin
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile learning-admin
aws ec2 describe-regions --profile learning-admin --output table
4.5 Output and Querying
aws ec2 describe-instances --region ap-south-1 --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].
[InstanceId,State.Name,InstanceType]' --output table
Server-side API filters and client-side query expressions reduce output and make scripts more
deterministic. Scripts must still handle empty responses, pagination, retries, non-zero exit codes, and
partial failures.
4.6 Credential Safety

Prefer federated or role-based temporary credentials for people and workloads.

Never embed credentials in source code, images, shell history, user data, or repositories.

Do not copy credentials into chat messages or tickets.

Use roles for EC2, containers, and Lambda rather than static access keys.

Rotate or revoke exposed credentials immediately and review CloudTrail activity.
4.7 CloudShell
AWS CloudShell provides a browser-based shell with AWS CLI and tools available. It is useful for quick
queries and learning.

Rotate or revoke exposed credentials immediately and review CloudTrail activity.
4.7 CloudShell
AWS CloudShell provides a browser-based shell with AWS CLI and tools available. It is useful for quick
queries and learning. Its convenience does not eliminate the need to verify account, Region, and
permissions, and important scripts should live in version control rather than only in the shell
environment.
4.8 SDK Concepts
import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError
session = boto3.Session(profile_name="learning-admin", region_name="ap-south-1")
ec2 = session.client("ec2")
try:
response = ec2.describe_instances()
for reservation in response.get("Reservations", []):
for instance in reservation.get("Instances", []):
print(instance["InstanceId"], instance["State"]["Name"])
except ClientError as exc:
print(f"AWS API error: {exc}")
raise
4.9 Automation Quality Requirements

Make operations idempotent where possible.

Log the account, Region, resource identifiers, and requested action.

Use dry-run or read-only discovery before destructive changes.

Handle throttling with bounded exponential backoff.

Use explicit timeouts and validate the final resource state.


Require human approval for high-impact production actions. Chapter Summary

The Console is valuable for learning, but CLI, SDK, and Infrastructure as Code provide repeatability.

Identity and Region verification are mandatory safety checks.

Temporary credentials and workload roles are safer than long-lived static keys. Interview Questions
1. When would you use CloudShell instead of a locally installed CLI?
2. What does aws sts get-caller-identity verify?
3. Why are named profiles useful?
4. What is a credential provider chain?
5. How should automation handle API throttling and partial failure?
6. Why is console-only production administration risky?
Hands-on Lab 4 - CLI Safety and Inventory
Objective: Create a safe CLI workflow for inventorying resources. Tasks
1. Install or open AWS CLI v2 and verify its version.
2. Authenticate using a delegated identity and run aws sts get-caller-identity.
3. List configured profiles and confirm the default Region.
4. Use a query expression to list EC2 instance IDs, states, and types in a table.
5. Export a read-only inventory result to JSON.
6. Write a shell function that prints identity and Region before running another AWS command. Validation

No root credentials or hard-coded keys are used.

The command output identifies the intended account and Region.

CHAPTER 5
Identity and Access Management Deep
Dive
Authorization policies, roles, federation, evaluation logic, and enterprise access design
Learning Objectives

Explain identities, policies, roles, trust policies, and sessions.

Read and write least-privilege IAM policies.

Apply policy evaluation logic, including explicit deny.

Use roles and temporary credentials for workloads and cross-account access.

Understand permission boundaries, service control policies, and federation.
5.1 Authentication and Authorization
Authentication proves the identity of a principal. Authorization determines whether that principal may
perform a requested action on a resource under stated conditions. A successful login does not imply
permission to every service.

5.3 Policy Anatomy
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "ReadProjectArtifacts",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-project-artifacts/*",
"Condition": {
"Bool": {"aws:SecureTransport": "true"}
}
}
]
}
A statement combines effect, action, resource, and optional conditions. Wildcards simplify policies but
expand the blast radius. Production policies should scope actions and resources as tightly as the service
supports.
5.4 Evaluation Logic
1. A request is denied by default.
2. Applicable identity-based and resource-based permissions are evaluated.
3. An explicit allow can grant access when no higher-level restriction blocks it.
4. An explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides an allow.
5. Permission boundaries, session policies, service control policies, and resource policies may reduce the
effective permission set. Key rule: A permission boundary does not grant permission. It limits the maximum permissions that an
identity-based policy may grant.
5.5 Roles and Trust
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [{
"Effect": "Allow",
"Principal": {"Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com"},
"Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
}]
}
The trust policy permits the EC2 service to assume the role. A separate permissions policy defines what the
resulting session may do. Trust and permission are separate questions: who may obtain the role, and what
may the role do?
5.6 Workload Identity
Applications running on AWS should receive credentials from an attached role or service-specific
workload identity mechanism. The platform supplies temporary credentials and rotates them. This avoids
distributing static secrets across servers, containers, and deployment pipelines.

5.7 Cross-Account Access
A principal in one account can assume a role in another account when the target role trust policy and the
source principal permissions both permit it. Cross-account roles support centralized workforce identity
and reduce duplicate users. External IDs, organization conditions, session tags, and source identity can
strengthen third-party and enterprise access patterns.
5.8 Federation and IAM Identity Center
Workforce users should usually authenticate through an organization identity provider and receive
temporary access through AWS IAM Identity Center or another federation pattern. Centralized
authentication improves lifecycle management, MFA enforcement, account access assignment, and
auditability.
5.9 Guardrails

Permission boundaries cap delegated IAM administration.

Service control policies in AWS Organizations restrict the maximum permissions available in member
accounts.

Resource policies control access directly on supported resources.

Conditions can require encryption, approved networks, MFA, tags, source accounts, or organization
membership.

Access Analyzer and policy simulation help discover unintended or missing access.
5.10 Least-Privilege Method
1. Define the job task and exact API operations.
2. Scope resources by ARN, account, Region, project, and environment where supported.
3. Add conditions for secure transport, source, tags, or session context.
4. Test denied and allowed scenarios.
5. Observe real activity and refine permissions.
6. Review periodically and remove unused access.


IAM separates authentication, trust, and authorization.

Roles and temporary sessions are the default production pattern for workforce and workload access.

Effective permissions are the intersection of grants and guardrails, with explicit deny taking
precedence. Interview Questions
1. What is the difference between a role trust policy and a permissions policy?
2. Explain IAM policy evaluation and explicit deny.
3. What does a permission boundary do?
4. How does cross-account role assumption work?

5. Why are roles preferable to access keys for EC2 applications?
6. Compare an IAM policy, resource policy, and service control policy.
7. How would you implement least privilege for a deployment pipeline?
Hands-on Lab 5 - Least-Privilege Role Design
Objective: Create and test a narrowly scoped read-only role. Tasks
1. Create a customer-managed policy that permits describing EC2 instances and reading selected
CloudWatch metrics.
2. Create a role with an appropriate trust policy for your test principal.
3. Assume the role and verify the session identity.
4. Test an allowed read action.
5. Test a denied write action such as starting or terminating an instance.
6. Review the access in CloudTrail or the available audit view.
7. Remove the test role and policy after validation. Validation

Allowed operations succeed and write operations fail.

The session uses temporary credentials.

The policy contains no unnecessary wildcard administrative actions.

CHAPTER 6
Amazon EC2 Compute Engineering
Instances, AMIs, families, purchasing models, bootstrapping, access, and operations
Learning Objectives

Explain the EC2 instance lifecycle and launch configuration.

Select instance families based on CPU, memory, storage, network, and accelerator needs.


Block storage presents addressable storage devices to an operating system. Filesystems and databases use
those blocks. Amazon EBS provides persistent block volumes for EC2. EBS volumes are created in an

incremental backups that can be used to create new volumes.

7.5 Resizing
Increasing EBS volume size does not automatically expand the partition or filesystem. After modifying the
volume, inspect the device, extend the partition when one exists, and grow the filesystem using the correct
operating-system tool. Validate both block-device and filesystem size afterward.
7.6 Snapshots
EBS snapshots are point-in-time, incremental backups. Crash-consistent snapshots capture the block state
at a moment, but application-consistent recovery may require filesystem freeze, database flush, backup
integration, or application quiescence. A snapshot is useful only when restoration is tested.

7.7 EBS Encryption
EBS encryption uses AWS KMS keys and protects data at rest, data moving between an instance and its
attached EBS storage, and subsequent encrypted snapshots. Encryption should normally be enabled by
default at the account and Region level, with key governance matching the workload’s compliance and
recovery requirements.

8.4 Health Checks
A health check must represent application readiness, not merely that a process exists. A useful endpoint
verifies critical local dependencies without causing expensive downstream work. Thresholds should avoid
both slow failure detection and unstable flapping. Health design: Separate liveness, readiness, and deep diagnostic signals. A load balancer readiness
check should answer whether the target can safely receive traffic now.
8.5 TLS and Traffic Paths
Application Load Balancers can terminate TLS using certificates. The target connection may use HTTP or
HTTPS depending on security requirements. Security groups should enforce the intended path: clients
reach the load balancer, and instances accept application traffic only from the load balancer security
group.
8.6 Auto Scaling Groups
An Auto Scaling group maintains a collection of EC2 instances between minimum, desired, and maximum
capacity. It launches instances from a launch template, monitors health, replaces unhealthy instances, and
changes capacity based on policies or schedules. When integrated with a load balancer, new instances
register and terminated instances deregister automatically.

9.1 VPC as a Network Boundary
Amazon Virtual Private Cloud provides a logically isolated virtual network. You select IP address ranges,
create subnets, configure route tables and gateways, attach security controls, and place resources into the
resulting network. A VPC belongs to one Region and spans its Availability Zones; each subnet belongs to
one AZ.
9.2 CIDR Planning
CIDR defines an address range and prefix length. A smaller prefix number represents a larger network. Address planning should reserve space for growth, multiple AZs, environment separation, and
connectivity to other VPCs or on-premises networks. Overlapping ranges complicate or prevent routing
between networks. Example

9.3 Subnets
A subnet becomes public or private because of its route-table path and resource addressing—not because
of its name. A public subnet commonly has a default route to an internet gateway, and internet-facing
resources require suitable public addressing.

resources require suitable public addressing. A private subnet lacks a direct inbound internet route. An
isolated subnet has no route to the internet and may contain data services.

9.4 Route Tables
Every subnet is associated with one route table. A route contains a destination and a target. AWS routing
uses the most specific matching route. The local route enables communication within the VPC CIDR. Default routes such as 0.0.0.0/0 direct traffic not matched by a more specific route. Public subnet route table

9.5 Internet Gateway
An internet gateway attaches to a VPC and can be the target of routes for internet traffic. A route alone is
not sufficient: instances also require public addressing where applicable, security rules, operating-system
listeners, and a valid return path.
9.6 NAT Gateway
A public NAT gateway placed in a public subnet allows resources in private subnets to initiate outbound
IPv4 internet connections without accepting unsolicited inbound internet connections. Private subnet
route tables point the default route to the NAT gateway, while the NAT gateway’s public subnet routes to
the internet gateway. Availability and cost: For resilient multi-AZ designs, use an appropriate NAT path per AZ and route
each private subnet locally. NAT gateways also have hourly and data-processing cost, so VPC endpoints
and architecture choices can reduce both dependency and expense.
9.7 VPC Endpoints
VPC endpoints provide private connectivity to supported AWS services without requiring traffic to
traverse an internet gateway or NAT gateway. Gateway endpoints and interface endpoints have different
architectures and pricing.

9.9 DNS and Addressing
VPC DNS settings, Route 53 Resolver, private hosted zones, and resource hostnames affect service
discovery. Production systems should use stable DNS names rather than hard-coded IP addresses. Public
IPv4 addresses and Elastic IP addresses should be assigned only when justified, monitored, and removed
when unused.
9.10 Flow Logs and Reachability
VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about network flows at supported interfaces, subnets, or VPC scope. They
help investigate accepted and rejected traffic but are not packet payload captures. Reachability analysis,
route inspection, security-group references, NACL rules, DNS testing, and application listeners together
support systematic troubleshooting.
9.11 Packet-Path Troubleshooting Method
1. Define source IP, source port, destination IP or DNS name, destination port, and protocol.
2. Resolve DNS and confirm the expected address.
3. Check the source route table and most-specific route.
4. Check gateway, endpoint, peering, VPN, or transit path state.
5. Check security-group egress and ingress rules.
6. Check NACL rules in both directions, including ephemeral ports.
7. Check destination listener and operating-system firewall.
8. Check return route and asymmetric-routing risk.
9. Use flow logs and application logs to validate the result. Chapter Summary

10.1 Cost Is an Architecture Property
AWS cost is created by architecture and operations: runtime hours or seconds, instance size, storage
capacity and performance, requests, data processing, public IP usage, load balancers, NAT gateways,
snapshots, logs, cross-AZ and internet data transfer, support plans, and managed-service consumption. Cost optimization begins during design and continues through measurement and ownership.

10.4 Optimization Levers

Rightsize compute based on observed CPU, memory, network, and storage behavior.

Scale horizontally and scale in when demand falls.

Stop non-production resources outside working hours when safe.

Use Spot for interruption-tolerant workloads.

Adopt commitments only after stable usage is understood.

Choose storage classes, volume types, snapshot retention, and log retention intentionally.

Reduce unnecessary cross-AZ, NAT, and internet data transfer.

Delete unattached volumes, stale snapshots, unused load balancers, and orphaned addresses.

Prefer managed services when reduced operations justifies their price.

Include engineering labor and risk in total cost of ownership.
10.5 Unit Economics
Total monthly cost alone does not show efficiency. Teams should track cost per useful business unit, such
as cost per request, active user, build, deployment, gigabyte processed, or order. Unit cost reveals whether
increased spend is caused by healthy growth or declining efficiency.
10.6 Governance Model
1. Assign every resource an owner and environment.
2. Use policy and automation to require key tags.
3. Establish budgets at account, project, and environment levels.
4. Review cost anomalies and untagged resources on a defined schedule.
5. Create approved service patterns and quotas.
6. Require expiry for temporary environments.
7. Measure optimization savings without weakening reliability or security.

6. Contain the cost safely without deleting evidence or production dependencies.
